sustainable-growth-rate.summary: Sustainable growth is modeled here as annual ROE multiplied by earnings retention. A 15% annual ROE and 40% dividend payout leave 60% retention and give a 9% SGR approximation. The result assumes stable policies and is not a prediction of actual sales growth.
sustainable-growth-rate.scope: An annual ROE × retention approximation for positive ROE, positive earnings/equity in accounting mode, and dividend payout from 0% to 100%. Fixed policy assumptions, no full financing model, new equity issuance, market feed, growth forecast or automatic valuation growth input.

examples.title: A 40% payout leaves 60% of earnings
examples.answer: The stated annual ROE × retention model gives 9%. It does not predict next year’s sales.

examples.title: Annual accounting inputs reproduce the same 9%
examples.inputs: net income: 180000; dividends: 72000; equity begin: 1000000; equity end: 1400000
steps: Average beginning and ending positive equity: ($1,000,000 + $1,400,000) / 2 = $1,200,000.
Current-year earnings retained are $108,000, and the same ROE × retention product is 9%.
examples.answer: The annual SGR approximation is 9%, using a two-point average equity base and matching income/dividend scope.

examples.title: Retain all earnings at unchanged ROE
examples.answer: SGR is 15% under the unchanged-ROE assumption. This is not a recommendation to stop dividends.

examples.title: Distribute all earnings in the equation
examples.answer: The result is 0%, rather than an undefined ratio. Real growth could still involve changes outside this model.

examples.title: Retention needed for a selected 12% target
examples.answer: An 80% retention assumption yields the selected 12% product. It does not establish the financing or investment needed to achieve it.

examples.title: The maximum feasible target at this ROE
steps: At unchanged 15% annual ROE, a 15% target requires 15 / 15 = 100% retention.
That corresponds to zero dividend payout.
examples.answer: The feasible upper boundary of this 0–100% retention model is 15%; a higher target is rejected.

questions.question: What formula does this SGR calculator use?
questions.answer: It uses annual SGR = annual ROE × earnings retention, where retention = 1 − dividend payout ratio. The accounting mode computes ROE with a two-point average of positive beginning and ending book equity. Other timing conventions are not silently substituted.

questions.question: Does sustainable growth mean the company cannot borrow?
questions.answer: No. The stated model assumes no new equity issuance and a stable capital structure; debt may rise proportionally with equity. A model forbidding all external financing is an internal-growth model and is not calculated here.

questions.question: What is the difference between retention and dividend payout?
questions.answer: For this positive-income scope, retention is the fraction of annual income not distributed as dividends. At 40% payout, retention is 60%. Current-year retained earnings are not the cumulative balance-sheet retained-earnings account or a cash-flow figure.

questions.question: Why does the calculator stop for losses or nonpositive equity?
questions.answer: Those inputs do not support the positive-earnings sustainable-growth interpretation used here. Accounting mode requires positive annual net income, positive beginning and ending equity, and dividends no greater than income.

questions.question: Can I set a target above the entered annual ROE?
questions.answer: That would require retention above 100% in this equation. The inverse mode rejects it instead of treating a negative dividend payout as feasible. Change the target or investigate whether a different ROE assumption is defensible.

questions.question: Can I use this output as perpetual dividend growth?
questions.answer: Do not transfer it automatically. A DDM or DCF stable-growth assumption needs its own support and a required return or discount rate above that perpetual growth rate. This SGR is conditional on the supplied profitability and retention assumptions.
